title: Everything Sunny All The Time Always

jokes.text: Lullaby lyrics: 'Hush, island baby / Tomorrow you'll shuck the cane / Your little fingers bloody / Prepare to be whipped'
jokes.setup: A baby is being sung to sleep — a classic tender parenting moment
jokes.punchline: The lullaby is about brutal colonial child labor, sung in a warm, soothing tone
jokes.explanation: A cold-open masterstroke. The warmth of the lullaby format collides violently with imagery of child plantation labor. It's perfectly Jack Donaghy — patrician, oblivious to moral horror, genuinely believing this is appropriate. The economy is exceptional: four short lines do enormous character and comedy work. Scores 8+ because it's both original and deeply character-specific.

jokes.text: Jack says 'Dr. Kevorkian says we have to put her down' — referring to his pediatrician
jokes.setup: Jack says the baby needs to sleep and quotes the doctor's orders
jokes.punchline: The doctor is named Dr. Kevorkian — the name of the famous euthanasia advocate — making 'put her down' suddenly sinister before Jack clarifies it's just an unfortunate name
jokes.explanation: Perfectly structured misdirection. 'Put her down' lands as a horror beat, then Jack's deadpan follow-up 'He's a very good pediatrician, but that is an unfortunate name' is the ideal punchline. The two-beat structure is clean and the callback to Dr. Kevorkian is culturally legible. High structure and economy scores because it's compact and perfectly timed.

jokes.text: 'Babynomics at 11:00' — Jack's daughter's scheduled class
jokes.setup: Jack refuses to wake the baby because she has a scheduled activity
jokes.punchline: The activity is 'Babynomics' — an absurd mashup of baby and economics, perfectly capturing Jack's obsessive drive to raise a miniature capitalist
jokes.explanation: A single invented word does enormous work — it tells us everything about Jack's parenting philosophy and gets a laugh purely through portmanteau. High character integration because only Jack would schedule economics classes for an infant. Economy is near-perfect: one word, one laugh.

jokes.text: Liz mistakes Tracy's urine for soda left behind in his apartment
jokes.setup: Liz complains that Tracy left a bunch of soda sitting out in his vacated apartment
jokes.punchline: Jenna clarifies: 'That's his urine. He is not well.'
jokes.explanation: The straight delivery of 'He is not well' is the perfect capper. It's gross but executed with complete deadpan, which elevates it. The economy is great — Jenna's two-sentence response does double duty as punchline and Tracy character note. Slightly below top tier because urine humor is a reliable but not original comedic device.

jokes.text: 'Someday this place is gonna be a kick-ass duplex, like on Diff'rent Strokes. Conrad Bain once slapped me in a men's room.'
jokes.setup: Liz envisions her dream apartment renovation
jokes.punchline: She references Diff'rent Strokes as a design inspiration, then abruptly reveals Conrad Bain (Mr. Drummond) once assaulted her in a restroom — a completely inexplicable non sequitur delivered as a mundane aside
jokes.explanation: 30 Rock's signature move: an absurd biographical non sequitur delivered as if it's completely normal. The Conrad Bain detail is so specific and random it achieves a kind of surreal comedy perfection. High quotability because the image is so bizarre and specific. The structure benefits from being tossed off casually — the lack of emphasis IS the joke.

jokes.text: Liz finds a half-finished Spanish study guide: 'Comencé a estudiar these, but then yo gave up.'
jokes.setup: Liz is going through old boxes of her stuff
jokes.punchline: She speaks the sentence mixing English and Spanish mid-sentence, demonstrating that she gave up on Spanish learning precisely where she stopped — the mixing of the two languages IS the evidence of the failure
jokes.explanation: Elegant self-demonstrating joke. The form (code-switching mid-sentence) IS the content (she gave up halfway through). Perfectly economic — one sentence, no explanation needed. Strong character integration because it speaks to Liz's pattern of ambitious self-improvement projects that fizzle.

jokes.text: Liz finds her unfinished novel. First line: 'Liz stabbed Jenna repeatedly.'
jokes.setup: Liz picks up her long-abandoned novel manuscript and reads the first line aloud
jokes.punchline: The opening line of the novel is just Liz stabbing Jenna — violent, petty, and autobiographically wish-fulfilling
jokes.explanation: Six words that simultaneously define Liz's relationship with Jenna, her creative process, and her deepest fantasy. The fact that this is the OPENING LINE of the novel (implying there's no artful setup — she just started with catharsis) is brilliant structural comedy. High character integration and quotability. Justifies 8+ because it's economically perfect and psychologically spot-on.

jokes.text: Jenna claims The Secret caused Gwyneth Paltrow to sing flat at the Oscars: 'I visualized all of that.'
jokes.setup: Jenna argues The Secret works, listing her successes as evidence
jokes.punchline: Her third example of The Secret working is that she wished for Gwyneth Paltrow to embarrass herself, and it came true — she claims credit for a public failure of a celebrity rival
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Jenna. The joke works on multiple levels: it's a real event (Gwyneth sang at the Oscars), Jenna interprets The Secret as a weapon for petty celebrity vendettas rather than self-improvement, and 'I visualized all of that' is delivered with total sincerity. Extremely high character integration because this joke could only come from Jenna. Justifies 8+ because it's original, character-specific, and genuinely surprising.

jokes.text: Jenna mishears 'taking action' as a reference to the drug 'Action': 'It dries your mouth out, but the sex is amazing.'
jokes.setup: Liz urges Jenna to start 'taking action' in her life
jokes.punchline: Jenna interprets it as a reference to a drug called 'Action' and gives a drug-review testimonial
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection wordplay. The drug review format ('dries your mouth out, but the sex is amazing') is delivered as a straightforward consumer report, which is the joke. Strong character integration — Jenna casually referencing drugs and sex as mundane facts of her life.

jokes.text: 'I always think of a third thing when I'm listing stuff.'
jokes.setup: Liz is mid-argument, structuring her points
jokes.punchline: She breaks from the argument to confess a personal verbal tic — and it's a meta-comment on the comedic rule of three
jokes.explanation: A quick, clever bit of meta self-awareness. It's a brief interruption of the argument's logic that comments on Liz's own thought patterns. Modest impact but sharp economy — one sentence, one laugh.

jokes.text: Liz notices she has a Post-it on her sweater — implying she's so disorganized she's been walking around with a reminder note stuck to herself
jokes.setup: Jenna challenges Liz on her chaotic personal life
jokes.punchline: Jenna points to a Post-it on Liz's sweater as evidence — a visual gag implying Liz can't even keep track of her own reminders
jokes.explanation: A well-executed visual gag. The Post-it on the sweater is physical evidence of Liz's personal chaos — perfect showing-not-telling. Rewatch bonus because it's a visual detail you may miss on first viewing.

jokes.text: Jenna demonstrates her Secret-powered Spanish fluency by threatening her housekeeper: 'Rosa, I know you stole my necklace. I'll have your son deported. Oh, wait. I found my necklace. Oh, boy.'
jokes.setup: Jenna claims The Secret made her fluent in Spanish and demonstrates
jokes.punchline: Her fluency is used entirely to level immigration threats at her housekeeper over a missing necklace that she immediately finds — a cascade of cringe moral horror played completely straight
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Perfect escalating structure: (1) Jenna brags about Secret-powered Spanish, (2) demonstrates by threatening her housekeeper with deportation, (3) immediately finds the necklace. The 'Oh, boy' at the end — Liz's characteristic self-aware groan adopted by Jenna — is a perfect capper. This is Jenna at maximum Jenna: oblivious, entitled, casually monstrous. Justifies 8+ because the three-beat structure is immaculate and the character specificity is total.

jokes.text: Jenna claims she used The Secret to learn Spanish; her demonstration is threatening her housekeeper Rosa with deportation over a necklace, then immediately retracting it
jokes.setup: Jenna says she used The Secret to become fluent in Spanish and demonstrates it
jokes.punchline: Her 'fluency' consists of threatening her housekeeper with deportation and then immediately going 'Oh wait, I found my necklace. Oh, boy.'
jokes.explanation: Outstanding character integration. Jenna's 'Spanish fluency' reveals her as wealthy, casually cruel, completely oblivious to the harm she causes, and immediately self-excusing ('Oh wait, I found it'). The 'Oh, boy' kicker mirrors Liz's catchphrase, adding another layer. This demonstrates The Secret's bankruptcy while being a devastating character portrait.

jokes.text: Liz introduces her life philosophy: 'Lizbeanism' — 'I'm Liz, and obviously, my philosophy is simple, like a bean.'
jokes.setup: Liz tells Jack she has a new life philosophy with an intentionally coined name
jokes.punchline: The name 'Lizbeanism' sounds like 'lesbianism,' but when Jack notes it with a raised eyebrow ('I see'), Liz's explanation is even funnier — she explains the 'bean' part refers to simplicity, completely missing the double entendre
jokes.explanation: A two-layer joke: the double entendre of the name and then Liz's blissfully oblivious explanation, which makes it funnier than if she'd intended the pun. Jack's understated 'I see' is perfect straight-man work. The bean explanation is absurd enough to be independently funny.

jokes.text: Liz announces 'Lizbeanism means that I am a dike...' — long pause — '...against the rising waters of mediocrity.'
jokes.setup: Liz continues explaining Lizbeanism with a metaphor
jokes.punchline: She appears to be about to use a slur/sexual term ('dike'), then completes it as a water-containment metaphor ('against the rising waters of mediocrity') — the pause is the joke
jokes.explanation: A masterclass in structural comedy — the episode notation [03:06] suggests a scene break/pause that IS the joke. The setup from Lizbeanism (#13) pays off here. The pause between 'I am a dike' and '...against the rising waters' is perfectly timed dramatic irony. Justifies 8+ for structure: the callback, the misdirection, and the payoff all work in concert.

jokes.text: Jack, after Liz's big speech about taking control: 'I'm going to give you...' [long pause] '...one of my neckties.'
jokes.setup: Jack appears moved by Liz's declaration of personal transformation, builds dramatic tension with a meaningful pause
jokes.punchline: He gives her a necktie — a mundane, gendered-wrong gift that deflates the moment while revealing Jack's actual value system
jokes.explanation: The pause between 'I'm going to give you' and 'one of my neckties' is dramatically built, and the deflation is perfect. A necktie communicates everything: Jack thinks this is meaningful, it's a masculine token, it's probably expensive but totally useless for Liz. The gap between his genuine emotion and the comic bathos of the gift is exquisite. This justifies 8+ for structure and character integration — it could only be Jack.

jokes.text: Jack recites Invictus inspirationally, then Liz asks: 'Wait, who was the white guy in that?' — referring to the film Invictus
jokes.setup: Jack delivers the Invictus poem with gravitas, and Liz recognizes the reference
jokes.punchline: Liz's takeaway is wondering who played the white character in the Clint Eastwood film — reducing a grand rhetorical moment to a casting question, and getting the racial framing backwards
jokes.explanation: Perfect Liz Lemon characterization: she deflates a soaring moment with a mundane, slightly-off-the-mark movie trivia question. The framing of 'the white guy' in a movie primarily about Mandela (played by Morgan Freeman) is the joke — she's missed the point of both the poem and the film.

jokes.text: Jack describes the privileges of success: 'having people pay you for the privilege of cutting your hair'
jokes.setup: Jack is describing what success looks like — power, wealth, privilege
jokes.punchline: One of his examples is that barbers pay HIM for the privilege of cutting his hair — an inversion of normal economics that reveals Jack's truly stratospheric self-regard
jokes.explanation: The reversal of the economic relationship (barbers paying Jack rather than vice versa) is economical absurdism that tells us everything about Jack's self-image. High character integration because this specific delusion fits Jack perfectly.

jokes.text: Liz: 'You're raising a child?' Jack: 'Come on. I think Avery is probably doing that.'
jokes.setup: Jack lists raising a child as one of his achievements
jokes.punchline: When Liz expresses surprise, Jack immediately disclaims responsibility with 'I think Avery is probably doing that' — maximum plausible deniability on parenthood
jokes.explanation: Quick, effective character beat. 'I think Avery is probably doing that' is a wonderfully non-committal answer about one's own child — the 'probably' is doing a lot of work. Functional rather than exceptional.

jokes.text: Liz invokes The Secret sarcastically; Jack: 'I wish Liz Lemon would leave so I could go back to work.' Liz is immediately dragged out by an unseen force, screaming.
jokes.setup: Liz warns Jack about The Secret's power; Jack dismisses it by making a wish
jokes.punchline: The Secret immediately works — Liz is physically yanked out of the room by an invisible force, narrating her own helpless exit
jokes.explanation: Delightful physical absurdism where the show commits to the bit. Jack's skeptical wish is granted instantly and literally, and Liz's running commentary ('Oh! I really fell! I need help!') as she's dragged out is perfectly executed. The willingness to go full physical comedy in a dialogue-heavy show makes this stand out.

jokes.text: 'I think I speak for all of us when I say how thrilled we... / Great impression of a guy that sucks, Dotcom!'
jokes.setup: Kenneth begins a heartfelt welcome-back speech for Tracy
jokes.punchline: Tracy immediately hijacks the moment to mock Dotcom instead — refusing the emotional beat in favor of dominance
jokes.explanation: Solid character comedy that efficiently establishes Tracy's dynamic with his entourage. The interruption of Kenneth's earnest speech is a good laugh, and 'Great impression of a guy that sucks' is a perfectly Tracy-esque non-insult insult.

jokes.text: 'Smooth move, Ferguson' — an inside joke from the entourage that Tracy doesn't understand
jokes.setup: Tracy returns and everyone is excited; after the welcome, one of the entourage says 'Smooth move, Ferguson' and everyone laughs
jokes.punchline: Tracy has no idea what this means — his own entourage has an inside joke he's excluded from
jokes.explanation: The episode's central recurring bit is introduced cleanly. Tracy's exclusion from his own entourage's joke is a clever inversion of the power dynamic — the man who commands absolute loyalty discovers that his servants have developed an inner life without him. Strong foundation for the running gag.

jokes.text: 'Smooth move, Ferguson.' [Grizz, Dotcom, and Kenneth burst out laughing; Tracy has no idea what this means]
jokes.setup: The entourage laughs at an inside joke Tracy doesn't understand
jokes.punchline: The complete exclusion of Tracy from his own entourage's private joke — the boss is left out
jokes.explanation: The launch of the episode's running gag. Works immediately because of the power inversion — Tracy's entourage exists entirely to serve him, so their laughter at something he doesn't understand is a perfect comic premise. The phrase itself ('Smooth move, Ferguson') is designed to sound funnier than it actually is.

jokes.text: Tracy: 'You three are not allowed to have inside jokes that I'm not a part of. I could have inside jokes that you're not a part of, for example, "Hot feet" or "Ask Melissa about it."'
jokes.setup: Tracy asserts that inside jokes are his exclusive privilege
jokes.punchline: He immediately demonstrates by citing two inside jokes of his own ('Hot feet,' 'Ask Melissa about it') — which are clearly just as meaningless to us as 'Smooth move, Ferguson' is to him, but he says them with complete authority
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Tracy's logic is perfectly unhinged: inside jokes are fine when HE has them, not when his entourage does. The specific invented examples ('Hot feet,' 'Ask Melissa about it') are funny precisely because they're opaque and we'll never learn their meaning. This is deeply Tracy — the solipsism is complete and internally consistent. Justifies 8+ for originality, character integration, and structure.

jokes.text: Tracy forbids 'Smooth move, Ferguson': 'it is not funny to me, so it is forbidden'
jokes.setup: Tracy declares 'Smooth move, Ferguson' forbidden
jokes.punchline: The logic: because HE doesn't find it funny, it cannot exist — the joke is Tracy's totalitarian comedic authority
jokes.explanation: Good extension of the running gag. The logic is pure Tracy — comedy is only legitimate if he approves it. Slightly lower than #23 because it's a follow-through beat rather than the original invention.

jokes.text: Grizz's DVD review: 'You wouldn't expect a movie called "Somewhere" to go absolutely nowhere.'
jokes.setup: Grizz delivers DVD reviews as part of the entourage's duties
jokes.punchline: A pun-based film review that actually works as criticism — 'Somewhere' goes 'nowhere'
jokes.explanation: A crisp pun that also functions as genuine film criticism (Sofia Coppola's 'Somewhere' was indeed criticized for being plotless). The meta-layer of Grizz being a film reviewer is itself funny. Great economy — the entire thing is one sentence.

jokes.text: Musical interlude: 'Sometimes we use a song to move a story along / And explain it to you / 'Cause Liz is taking charge...'
jokes.setup: Scene transition that needs to cover a time jump in Liz's storyline
jokes.punchline: The show breaks into a literal musical number with lyrics explaining the plot, openly admitting they're using the song as an expository device
jokes.explanation: A rare fully meta moment where 30 Rock acknowledges its own narrative conventions by turning them into a literal musical number. 'Sometimes we use a song to move a story along' is the show winking hard at the camera. Fresh and unexpected, though lower character integration because it's more of a structural gag than a character gag.

jokes.text: City worker: 'If you're not in the building, I don't have to talk to you.' — Liz shouts from outside about the bag in a tree
jokes.setup: Liz confronts a city worker about a bag stuck in the tree outside her window
jokes.punchline: The worker's bureaucratic dodge — he only has to talk to her if she's in the building — is a perfect example of city-worker logic
jokes.explanation: A functional joke about bureaucratic absurdity. Not especially original but gets the scene going. Below average for this episode's standards.

jokes.text: Avery video-calls expecting Skype sex; Jack is using the same device for the baby's FaceTime with mommy
jokes.setup: Jack sets up a video call so baby Liddy can see her mother
jokes.punchline: Avery arrives on screen already announcing 'Who's ready for Skype sex?' — not realizing the baby is watching
jokes.explanation: Classic crossed-wires comedy. The horror of 'Who's ready for Skype sex?' directed at a baby (from the baby's POV) is well-executed. Good structure, not exceptional.

jokes.text: 'You people have too much money.' — Sherry's reaction to the multiple video screens
jokes.setup: The elaborate baby-viewing video setup is revealed
jokes.punchline: A third-party character (Sherry) delivers the audience surrogate line about the absurdity of this wealth display
jokes.explanation: A functional audience-surrogate joke, but not particularly clever. It explains what the show wants us to feel rather than letting the absurdity speak for itself. Below average.

jokes.text: Jack insists he doesn't know why Liddy would be afraid of Reagan, then defensively asks: 'Are you accusing me of not doing enough Reagan time with her?'
jokes.setup: The baby apparently has a fear of something (implied: a picture or photo of Reagan)
jokes.punchline: Jack interprets the baby's fear of Reagan as a parenting failure on HIS part — 'Reagan time' is a scheduled activity for his infant daughter
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character joke. 'Reagan time' as a scheduled infant activity is perfectly Jack Donaghy — he has a curriculum for his baby that includes Ronald Reagan exposure. The defensive framing ('Are you accusing me of not doing enough...') mirrors how real parents feel guilty about screen time, but with Reagan. Justifies 8+ for originality and character integration.

jokes.text: Avery: 'Do you want to watch me eat jelly beans... real slow?' Jack: 'Yes.'
jokes.setup: Avery tries to initiate long-distance intimacy with Jack via video call
jokes.punchline: Her offer of watching her eat jelly beans 'real slow' as a form of Skype seduction — and Jack's sincere 'Yes' — is an oddly specific and perfectly committed bit
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'jelly beans... real slow' as the chosen erotic act is perfect. It's simultaneously wholesome and somehow transgressive. Jack's one-word sincere 'Yes' closes it perfectly. Economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: Tracy catches his entourage saying 'Smooth move, Ferguson' behind his back — having hidden to spy on them
jokes.setup: Tracy insisted they stop; the entourage resumed the joke the moment they thought he was gone
jokes.punchline: Tracy reveals he's been hiding to catch them in the act — and demands they explain why the joke is funny
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of the running gag. Tracy's surveillance and demand for an explanation is a perfect comedic power play. The joke deepens the absurdity of trying to recreate comedy for someone who wasn't there.

jokes.text: The explanation of 'Smooth move, Ferguson': 'the delivery guy tripped, and then Mr. Griswald said, "Smooth move, Ferguson."' Tracy: 'That story is not funny.'
jokes.setup: Tracy demands the story behind the joke; it's explained deadpan
jokes.punchline: The explanation is completely mundane and unfunny — and Tracy correctly identifies this, but it doesn't matter because 'you had to be there'
jokes.explanation: Meta comedy gold. The show explicitly deconstructs how inside jokes work: the story is objectively unfunny, but context makes it hilarious to those who were there. Tracy's flat 'That story is not funny' is correct, which makes it funnier. This is 30 Rock at its most self-aware about the mechanics of comedy. Justifies 8+ because it simultaneously IS the joke and IS ABOUT the joke.

jokes.text: Tracy's solution: 'We are going to re-create all the events surrounding "Smooth move, Ferguson" exactly as they occurred. Maybe then we can get on with our lives.'
jokes.setup: Tracy is told you had to be there
jokes.punchline: His solution is to reconstruct the entire historical event so he can retroactively 'be there' — treating an inside joke with the gravitas of a war crimes tribunal recreation
jokes.explanation: Exceptional. Tracy's decision to reconstruct the incident to retroactively experience the joke is absurd escalation at its finest. 'Maybe then we can get on with our lives' treats this trivial comedy dispute as a genuine psychological wound requiring forensic reconstruction. This is Tracy Jordan at peak Tracy — the insane logic is ironclad within his worldview. Justifies 8+ clearly.

jokes.text: Jonathan: 'Sir, you need to see this, even if it ruins whatever you had planned for Secretary's Day, like a poem you wrote for me or whatever.'
jokes.setup: Jonathan needs to interrupt Jack with urgent news
jokes.punchline: Jonathan assumes Jack was planning a heartfelt Secretary's Day poem for him — an example of Jonathan's delusional belief in his special relationship with Jack
jokes.explanation: Perfect Jonathan characterization. His sycophantic delusion ('a poem you wrote for me or whatever') and the casual dismissal of that fantasy in the same breath is very Jonathan. 'Or whatever' is doing great comic work — he's embarrassed to hope but can't help himself.

jokes.text: Kim Jong-il's pre-taped statement: 'world's greatest golfer and movie director and best man at Tom Brady's wedding'
jokes.setup: Kim Jong-il delivers a formal propaganda statement identifying himself
jokes.punchline: His credentials include being 'the world's greatest golfer and movie director' (actual North Korean propaganda claims) plus 'best man at Tom Brady's wedding' — an absurd celebrity insertion
jokes.explanation: The joke escalates perfectly: real propaganda (golf, movies) → absurd celebrity cameo (Tom Brady's best man). The escalation and the specificity of Tom Brady makes it work. Justified 8+ because the structure of mixing real propaganda claims with celebrity insertion is original and well-executed.

jokes.text: Kim Jong-il: 'the decadent Western journalist spy Laura Ling left us because she can't party as hard as we can'
jokes.setup: Kim Jong-il references the real Laura Ling hostage situation
jokes.punchline: His characterization of her imprisonment as a 'party' she wasn't tough enough for — reframing forced detention as an exclusive social event she couldn't keep up with
jokes.explanation: Dark and clever. The reframing of political detention as a party you failed to handle is sharp satirical writing. Putting words like this in a dictator's mouth while making them sound like frat bro talk is a specific comedic angle that works.

jokes.text: Kim Jong-il and aide: 'I know, right? / I know, right?' — North Korean response to the party claim
jokes.setup: Kim Jong-il makes a boast and glances to an aide
jokes.punchline: The totalitarian dictator and his subordinate engage in the most casual American millennial affirmation ('I know, right?') — a collision of register
jokes.explanation: Perfect register collision. Casual contemporary American slang from a North Korean dictator and his aide is funny through incongruity. The repetition (both saying it) amplifies it. Economy is near-perfect — three words, double-delivered.

jokes.text: Kim Jong-il: North Korea is 'awesome and we have enough food'
jokes.setup: Kim Jong-il promotes North Korea to an international audience
jokes.punchline: His pitch includes the baseline claim 'we have enough food' — an absurdly low bar that reveals the actual state of North Korea while pretending it's a selling point
jokes.explanation: The low bar of 'we have enough food' as a tourist pitch works because it indicts the reality of North Korean famine through the very act of denial. Sharp political satire in five words.

jokes.text: Kim Jong-il: 'Her name is Avery Jessup, and, like me, her hair is blond!'
jokes.setup: Kim Jong-il introduces the captured Western journalist
jokes.punchline: The thing he finds most notable to share about her is that they both have blond hair — an insane vanity detail from the dictator
jokes.explanation: A perfect absurdist reveal. Kim Jong-il is dark-haired in reality (the actor is wearing a wig), so claiming shared blond hair with Avery Jessup is a delusional vanity claim that's also a dig at North Korean propaganda's reality-denial. The exclamation mark sells his pride in this. One of the episode's funniest lines.

jokes.text: Jack upon learning Avery is detained: 'I told her to stay. I didn't want her at home. This is my fault.' Jonathan: 'Sir, if you say one more syllable, that's a haiku.'
jokes.setup: Jack is in shock and begins a three-sentence self-recrimination
jokes.punchline: Jonathan points out that Jack's three-sentence confession is exactly one syllable away from a haiku — then Jack says 'Leave' which completes it
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's finest moments. The joke has multiple layers: (1) Jonathan spots the haiku structure in Jack's genuine distress, (2) the observation itself is a tone-perfect interruption, (3) Jack says 'Leave' which completes the haiku. It earns its 9+ because it requires the audience to do the syllable count, rewards those who do, and the structural payoff (Jack's 'Leave' completing the poem) is an earned bonus. Near-perfect economy. The joke AND the verification of the joke happen simultaneously.

jokes.text: The news anchor pivots from Avery's kidnapping to: 'But first, it's never too early to plan your dog's Halloween costume.'
jokes.setup: Breaking news that an NBC journalist has been detained in North Korea
jokes.punchline: Immediate pivot to a dog Halloween costume segment — perfect satire of TV news priorities
jokes.explanation: Sharp media satire. The contrast is extreme enough to work well. Not particularly original as a news-satire move (The Simpsons/SNL have done similar) but efficiently executed with great economy.

jokes.text: Liz arrives at City Hall and is immediately warned: 'Don't go in there! Run, citizen!'
jokes.setup: Liz walks toward City Hall determined to fight the bureaucracy
jokes.punchline: A random citizen warns her off as if City Hall is a dangerous monster — implying bureaucratic horror so bad it causes genuine fear
jokes.explanation: A quick absurdist beat. The citizenry fleeing City Hall in terror is a good visual joke but doesn't reach the heights of the episode's better moments. Functional.

jokes.text: Liz interrupts Jack's Kim Jong-il crisis to ask for help with a bag stuck in a tree. Jack treats both problems as equally serious.
jokes.setup: Jack is dealing with an international hostage crisis involving his wife
jokes.punchline: Liz presents a bag stuck in a tree as if it's comparable, and Jack — after hearing both — treats them with equal philosophical seriousness
jokes.explanation: The tonal juxtaposition of nuclear-level geopolitical crisis vs. bag-in-tree is the episode's central comic engine. Jack's willingness to engage both with equal gravity is perfect Jack Donaghy.

jokes.text: Liz interrupts Jack's international kidnapping crisis with: 'Jack, I have a bag stuck in a tree outside my apartment'
jokes.setup: Jack is trying to get his wife freed from North Korea
jokes.punchline: Liz's complete absence of self-awareness in bringing her trivial complaint to Jack in this moment — and treating it as parallel in urgency
jokes.explanation: A good character beat that works because of the extreme disproportion between their problems. Jack's acknowledgment that they're facing 'similar situations' is the real joke — him granting her problem equal weight while his wife is in a North Korean prison.

jokes.text: North Korean news: 'And in food news, you've had enough to eat today. Now here with the weather is Johnny Mountain.'
jokes.setup: A North Korean news broadcast plays in the background
jokes.punchline: The food news segment is a simple decree that citizens have had enough food — the news functions as government command rather than reporting
jokes.explanation: Sharp political satire. 'You've had enough to eat today' reframes government dictate as news, and the casual transition 'Now here with the weather is Johnny Mountain' treats this totalitarian declaration as routine broadcast. Excellent economy and originality.

jokes.text: North Korean weather report: 'North Korea, everything sunny all the time always! Good time beach party! Back to you, Alereeb!'
jokes.setup: The North Korean weather segment follows the food news
jokes.punchline: The weather is uniformly declared perfect ('everything sunny all the time always') in a country where weather is clearly not controlled — propaganda extending even to meteorology
jokes.explanation: The episode title comes from this line, which gives it special status. 'Everything sunny all the time always' is perfectly over-committed propaganda. 'Good time beach party' adds absurdist energy. High quotability as the episode's title phrase.

jokes.text: Liz: 'What? Why? Is she a spy? Oh, my God, I already know too much!'
jokes.setup: Jack reveals Avery has been kidnapped by Kim Jong-il
jokes.punchline: Liz's immediate leap to 'Is she a spy?' and then her panicked 'Oh my God, I already know too much!' — treating it as a spy thriller danger to herself
jokes.explanation: A great Liz Lemon character beat — she immediately makes a crisis about herself (her own safety, spy thriller paranoia). 'I already know too much!' is very quotable and captures her nervous, TV-referential worldview. The escalation from genuine question to self-centered panic is quick and funny.

jokes.text: Avery can't accept Bill Clinton's help 'because she can't forgive him for not hitting on her during the 1996 Democratic Convention. She's much too thin.'
jokes.setup: Liz suggests calling President Clinton to negotiate for Avery's release
jokes.punchline: Avery's grudge against Clinton is that he DIDN'T hit on her — an inversion of the usual Clinton complaint — and Jack's deadpan addendum 'She's much too thin' implies Clinton only pursued a certain body type
jokes.explanation: The episode's single best joke. The inversion is perfect: the usual Clinton joke is about inappropriate advances, but this reverses it so Avery is OFFENDED at being skipped. Then Jack's addendum 'She's much too thin' simultaneously characterizes Avery's body type, Clinton's alleged 'type,' and Jack's own patrician delivery. Three layers of comedy in two sentences. Genuinely exceptional writing that subverts a well-worn cultural touchstone in an original direction. This is the anchor 9+ moment for this episode.

jokes.text: Jack broke up with Condoleezza Rice via text: 'Me plus you equals frowny face.'
jokes.setup: Jack reveals he dated Condoleezza Rice and broke it off badly
jokes.punchline: His breakup text was 'Me plus you equals frowny face' — a childishly emoji-logic message sent to the Secretary of State
jokes.explanation: Close competition with joke #45 for episode MVP. The collision of the relationship (Jack and the Secretary of State), the medium (text message), and the content ('Me plus you equals frowny face') is extraordinary. The emoji-math grammar of the text is perfect — childlike, cowardly, and somehow the most Jack Donaghy thing imaginable. This is what 9+ looks like: high originality, immaculate structure, total character integration, perfect economy. The phrase itself is instantly quotable and has a rhythmic quality that sticks.

jokes.text: Kenneth reports logistics obstacles: 'Dotcom licks the subway steps.' Tracy: 'These are solvable problems.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth lists why the re-creation is difficult (weather, clothing, etc.)
jokes.punchline: One of the variables is that Dotcom was sick — due to licking the subway steps — and Tracy treats this as a routine problem to engineer around
jokes.explanation: The throwaway 'Dotcom licks the subway steps' is delivered with zero editorializing — it's just a fact of this world. Tracy's 'These are solvable problems' without addressing the subway-licking at all is perfect deadpan. High originality for the specificity of the detail.

jokes.text: Jenna's hair re-growth for the re-creation: 'J-Mo, how long would it take for your hair to grow back?' / 'It depends. Do you have access to horse semen?' / 'You know I do.'
jokes.setup: Tracy learns Jenna got a haircut between the incident and now, disrupting the re-creation
jokes.punchline: Jenna offers a horse-semen hair growth solution; Tracy immediately confirms he has access to horse semen
jokes.explanation: Two-beat absurdist joke. Jenna offering horse semen as a hair solution is eccentric but the real joke is Tracy's instant 'You know I do' — confirming he just has horse semen available, no explanation offered or needed. The 'you know I do' implies this is common knowledge in their world. Excellent character integration for both.

jokes.text: Tracy: 'Then, we'll reconvene in three weeks! Meeting is adjourned! Oh, my God! What happened to my bug?'
jokes.setup: Tracy has just formally adjourned the recreation meeting
jokes.punchline: He immediately pivots from CEO-mode to panicked concern about a bug he was apparently watching — completely breaking the authority he just performed
jokes.explanation: A sharp character beat. The transition from formal 'Meeting is adjourned' to 'What happened to my bug?' is a perfect Tracy moment — the grandiosity deflating instantly into childlike distraction.

jokes.text: Liz: 'Stupid grappling hook! Can't catch one little bag?'
jokes.setup: Liz escalates her bag-retrieval operation with increasingly absurd tools
jokes.punchline: She's deployed a grappling hook to retrieve a plastic bag from a tree — massive overkill for a mundane problem, delivered with total indignation
jokes.explanation: The escalation of Liz's bag obsession reaches grappling-hook level, which is good. The indignant addressing of the hook ('Stupid grappling hook!') as if it's letting her down is a nice character beat.

jokes.text: Liz argues with the bag: 'You will not win, Mr. Bag!' The bag responds: 'But, Liz, I already have.'
jokes.setup: Liz has anthropomorphized the bag and is arguing with it
jokes.punchline: The bag talks back with a Hannibal Lecter-style confident reply — 'But, Liz, I already have'
jokes.explanation: The show commits to the anthropomorphized bag with remarkable confidence. 'But, Liz, I already have' is a villain monologue moment delivered by a plastic grocery bag. The absurdism is perfectly calibrated — the bag's menace is played straight. Justifies 8+ for the willingness to go this weird and execute it cleanly.

jokes.text: The bag monologue: 'No human is truly the master of his fate... I'm reminding you of your mortality... the wind rustling against my genitals. That's right, bags have genitals. You don't know me.'
jokes.setup: The bag continues its philosophical lecture to Liz
jokes.punchline: The bag's existential claims escalate to 'the wind rustling against my genitals. That's right, bags have genitals. You don't know me.' — a masterpiece of absurdist escalation
jokes.explanation: One of the most original moments in the episode. The bag's pivot from mortality philosophy to the casual assertion that 'bags have genitals' — followed by the defensive 'You don't know me' — is surreal comedy at a very high level. 'You don't know me' from a bag is a perfect comedic non sequitur that somehow feels earned. The episode commits to this bit with complete conviction. Justifies 9+ for originality — this is not a type of joke seen elsewhere.

jokes.text: The bag: 'Go ahead, buy nesting tables. Paint an accent wall. I'll watch the EMTs take you out in my cousin, a body bag.'
jokes.setup: The bag continues taunting Liz with existential dread
jokes.punchline: The bag reveals that body bags are its cousins — it has family relationships with medical equipment — and will watch Liz's death with familial solidarity
jokes.explanation: The body-bag-as-cousin twist is exceptional. The bag's threat is delivered with real menace — 'my cousin, a body bag' — while the concept of bags having family relationships is maximally absurd. This moment earns its high score because the punchline ('my cousin, a body bag') is genuinely surprising and works on both the horror and absurdist levels simultaneously.

jokes.text: Tracy, directing the re-creation: 'Was Dotcom standing that gay? No, sir, he was not.'
jokes.setup: Tracy is obsessively directing every detail of the re-creation
jokes.punchline: He demands precision on how gay Dotcom was standing — a specific directorial note that implies 'gayness of stance' is a quantifiable variable he's tracking
jokes.explanation: Tracy's directorial obsession continues. The specificity of the question (quantifying Dotcom's stance on a gay-to-straight scale) and the matter-of-fact answer is Tracy absurdism. Slightly lower for earned_vs_cheap because the joke flirts with using gay as a punchline, though the framing makes it more about Tracy's manic directorial precision.

jokes.text: Tracy recognizes Kim Jong-il: 'Hey, what's my boy KJ doing on TV?' / 'That's Kim Jong-il.' / 'Yeah. We did a movie together that he directed and co-starred in.'
jokes.setup: The news broadcast shows Kim Jong-il footage; Tracy recognizes him
jokes.punchline: Tracy casually reveals he made a film with Kim Jong-il — knowing the dictator as 'KJ,' his personal acquaintance
jokes.explanation: Brilliant character joke. Only Tracy Jordan would know Kim Jong-il as 'my boy KJ' and have made a movie with him. The casualness — 'Yeah. We did a movie together' — is perfect Tracy. High character integration because this revelation is absurd but 100% consistent with who Tracy is.

jokes.text: Clip from Tracy and Kim Jong-il's propaganda film: 'Death to the CIA! Let us all increase production of millet and sunflowers! I defuse bomb, black partner. Hasta la vista, baby.'
jokes.setup: We see a clip from the film Tracy made with Kim Jong-il
jokes.punchline: The clip is propaganda mixed with buddy-cop tropes — Kim Jong-il uses 'Hasta la vista, baby' while the film commands sunflower production
jokes.explanation: The film clip is a miniature masterpiece: state propaganda grafted onto American buddy-cop genre conventions ('black partner,' 'Hasta la vista, baby'). The specific detail of 'increase production of millet and sunflowers' grounds it in actual North Korean propaganda while 'I defuse bomb, black partner' captures the American action movie template. Sharp and original.

jokes.text: Tracy: 'It was either that or play a rapping doorman in a Kate Hudson movie.' — explaining why he did the North Korean propaganda film
jokes.setup: Dotcom points out Tracy appeared to do a North Korean propaganda film
jokes.punchline: Tracy's defense is that his alternative was a rapping doorman in a Kate Hudson movie — implying the propaganda film was actually the more dignified option
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke about Hollywood racism and the limited roles available to Black actors. The comparison — totalitarian propaganda vs. rapping doorman in a Kate Hudson romcom — positions Hollywood stereotyping as equivalent to or worse than working for a dictator. High originality and sharp social commentary disguised as Tracy absurdism. 'Rapping doorman' is a perfect specific detail. Justifies 8+ clearly.

jokes.text: The re-creation works perfectly and Tracy laughs: 'I get it now! It's so funny! Everyone, laugh! Now, you sons of bitches!'
jokes.setup: The elaborate re-creation has finally worked and Tracy experiences the joke
jokes.punchline: Tracy's response to finally finding it funny is to immediately command everyone else to laugh — converting genuine amusement into totalitarian decree
jokes.explanation: The perfect payoff to the episode's longest running gag. Tracy's transition from genuine laughter to 'Everyone, laugh! Now, you sons of bitches!' is pure Tracy — he can't just enjoy the moment, he has to command it. The 'you sons of bitches' is perfectly timed. This resolves a multi-act structure beautifully. Justifies 8+ for the payoff to all the setup.

jokes.text: Tracy briefs Jack on Kim Jong-il: 'Kim Jong-il sometimes shoots in the closeup too much. Comedy lives in the wide shot. And also... his acting notes are often vague.'
jokes.setup: Jack asks Tracy to tell him what Avery might be going through — implying he wants to know about conditions in North Korea
jokes.punchline: Tracy only knows Kim Jong-il as a director and actor, so his 'intelligence' is entirely a film review of the man's directorial style
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's finest moments. Jack asks about Avery's suffering in North Korean captivity; Tracy provides professional film criticism of Kim Jong-il's directorial choices. 'Comedy lives in the wide shot' as a piece of intelligence about a dictator is genuinely brilliant. The joke lands because Tracy is entirely sincere — his expertise IS film production, and that's how he knows KJ. High marks across the board. Justifies 9+ for originality and character integration.

jokes.text: 'We do a lot of pirate-themed sexual role-play. I'm a parrot.'
jokes.setup: Jack explains that Avery's 'floggings' match their sexual roleplay
jokes.punchline: 'I'm a parrot' — the specific, casual disclosure that Jack plays a parrot in their pirate BDSM
jokes.explanation: Four words that may be the episode's most perfectly economical joke. Jack Donaghy — patrician, powerful, self-serious — calmly announcing he plays a parrot in pirate sexual roleplay is the Platonic ideal of character-based absurdism. The economy is perfect (10/10): 'I'm a parrot' contains everything. The deadpan delivery makes it transcendent. This competes with joke #46 for episode MVP.

jokes.text: Avery concludes 'capitalism may be flawed.' Jack: 'My God! What are those monsters doing to her?'
jokes.setup: Avery has survived floggings and concrete-breaking without Jack's concern; these were normal to her
jokes.punchline: The single thing that horrifies Jack is Avery expressing doubt about capitalism — everything else was fine, but this is the true torture
jokes.explanation: Perfect payoff to the extended Avery captivity sequence. The three-beat structure (flogging = fine, concrete = fine, capitalism doubts = HORROR) is immaculate. Jack's 'My God! What are those monsters doing to her?' in response only to the capitalism comment is his character in a nutshell. Justifies 8+ clearly.

jokes.text: Condi Rice to Jack: 'You know, I've been to the DMZ. They have signs. Can your wife not read?'
jokes.setup: Condi confronts Jack about needing her help
jokes.punchline: Her first response is to insult Avery's literacy — pointing out there are DMZ warning signs, implying Avery walked into North Korea despite clear instructions
jokes.explanation: Condi's entrance line is sharp. The DMZ-signs-literacy attack is a perfect power move — it's both factually correct (there are signs) and a devastating put-down of a rival. The casual cruelty is very 30 Rock. 'Can your wife not read?' as a diplomatic opening gambit is original and character-specific.

jokes.text: Condi's jealous interrogation: 'Is she funnier than I am? She's certainly not younger, is she?'
jokes.setup: Condi, supposedly a serious diplomat, begins interrogating Jack about Avery
jokes.punchline: The Secretary of State is primarily concerned with how she compares to Avery in terms of humor and youth — reducing international diplomacy to romantic rivalry
jokes.explanation: The comedy of a powerful historical figure reduced to petty romantic jealousy is well-executed. 'Is she funnier than I am?' specifically is a surprising question to ask about a romantic rival.

jokes.text: Jack's list of apologies to Condi includes: 'I went drinking with Karl Rove on Valentine's Day' and 'I said your favorite movie was lame. "Mars Attacks!" is awesome!'
jokes.setup: Jack and Condi trade apologies for relationship failures
jokes.punchline: Jack's apologies escalate from the text breakup to drinking with Karl Rove on Valentine's Day to calling 'Mars Attacks!' lame — a cascade of increasingly specific political and pop culture grievances
jokes.explanation: 'Mars Attacks! is awesome!' from Condoleezza Rice — a detail that gives her a full, surprising personality — is a gem. Karl Rove on Valentine's Day is also a specific enough detail to get a laugh through sheer precision. The list structure escalates perfectly.

jokes.text: Condi and Jack's piano/flute grudge match: 'Now, admit that I'm better at the piano than you are at the flute.' / 'Never!' — followed by an actual musical duel
jokes.setup: Jack and Condi's argument escalates through romantic grievances
jokes.punchline: The entire confrontation culminates in a piano-vs-flute duel — two powerful characters settling geopolitical negotiations through competitive musical performance
jokes.explanation: The escalation to a musical duel is perfectly absurd. 'Never!' as a response to the piano admission question is a great comedic beat. The fact that they actually have the duel (implied by the scene structure) commits to the absurdism. Note: Condoleezza Rice is actually a skilled pianist in real life, giving this extra satirical bite.

jokes.text: Jack: 'Follow this, you turkey!' [during musical duel]
jokes.setup: Jack plays something on the piano during the musical competition
jokes.punchline: 'Follow this, you turkey!' is a magnificently absurd competitive taunt from Jack Donaghy — 'turkey' as an insult is archaic and unexpected
jokes.explanation: Jack's competitive trash talk using 'turkey' as an insult is charming and period-incongruous. It's a small but funny detail within the duel sequence.

jokes.text: Post-duel: Condi concedes Jack is better at piano. 'Now, get out of here before this gets weird.' / Jack: 'You're the turkey.'
jokes.setup: The musical duel concludes with Condi's concession
jokes.punchline: Condi's 'before this gets weird' — as if a piano duel between ex-lovers to negotiate hostage release isn't already weird — and Jack's parting 'You're the turkey' (a callback to earlier 'Follow this, you turkey!' from the duel) is absurd but perfect
jokes.explanation: 'Before this gets weird' when it's already maximally weird is good irony. 'You're the turkey' as a parting shot has the right nonsensical dignity. Good closing beat to the Condi sequence.

jokes.text: Liz: 'You will eat your family!' — to the bag she's planning to fill with other bags
jokes.setup: Liz finally gets the bag and announces her revenge plan
jokes.punchline: Her plan — hanging the bag in her kitchen and filling it with other bags — is framed as making it eat its family, a dark logic that treats bags as sentient kin
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the bag's family-tree revelation (body bag cousin) returns here as Liz's revenge. 'You will eat your family!' is a genuinely surprising and brilliant callback — the bag's family is other bags, and using bags-within-a-bag becomes cannibalism. The callback is earned and the dark logic is airtight. Extremely quotable. High originality for the payoff mechanics.

jokes.text: Cop threatens to tase Liz: 'Don't think I won't taser you, all right? I got OCD, and I love doing paperwork.'
jokes.setup: A cop intervenes as Liz chainsaws the tree to get the bag
jokes.punchline: His threat to tase her is amplified by the reveal that he WANTS to do the subsequent paperwork — his OCD makes tasing people a win for him
jokes.explanation: A great subversion: 'Don't think I won't taser you' becomes more threatening when paired with 'I love doing paperwork.' The OCD detail explains why this cop is MORE dangerous than a normal cop — he wants an excuse to fill out forms. Good economy and originality.

jokes.text: Avery: 'Nobody here's ever seen an iPhone. I told them it was my razor. I have to shave my legs with it, but they have an app for that.'
jokes.setup: Avery explains how she has a secret phone
jokes.punchline: She's committed to the razor cover story to the point of actually using the iPhone as a razor — and there's an app for that
jokes.explanation: A three-beat joke with a perfect button. (1) iPhone disguised as razor, (2) she actually shaves with it to maintain cover, (3) 'they have an app for that' — the 'there's an app for that' iPhone campaign tagline applied to leg shaving. Structure is excellent because each beat escalates and the button is a pop culture callback that's also character-specific (Avery is committed enough to actually shave with a phone).

jokes.text: Avery: 'That pansy Harry Truman for not taking down this country when he had the chance.'
jokes.setup: Jack says this is nobody's fault; Avery disagrees
jokes.punchline: Avery blames Truman for not destroying North Korea when he had the opportunity — a casually hawkish political opinion delivered from inside North Korean captivity
jokes.explanation: Avery's character is perfectly crystallized: held captive in North Korea, her takeaway is that Truman was a 'pansy' for not bombing the country out of existence when he could. 'Pansy Harry Truman' is a great specific detail. High character integration — only Avery Jessup-Donaghy holds this specific view.

jokes.text: Avery: 'They actually love me here. I already won a North Korean Emmy.'
jokes.setup: Avery reassures Jack she's okay and has adapted
jokes.punchline: She's won a North Korean Emmy — a meaningless propaganda award she's treated as a genuine professional achievement
jokes.explanation: 'I already won a North Korean Emmy' is a perfect sentence — it's absurd and specific, and it tells us that Avery's competitive drive to win awards has continued even in captivity. She's thriving in a totalitarian state because she's good at state propaganda.

jokes.text: Avery: 'Did you also call Sally Ride and her sister?' — jealous that Jack called Condi
jokes.setup: Jack mentions he spoke to Condoleezza; Avery reacts
jokes.punchline: Her jealous response references Sally Ride (implying she's another one of Jack's powerful-woman exes) and adds 'her sister' as an escalation
jokes.explanation: A quick joke extending Jack's history of powerful ex-girlfriends. 'Sally Ride and her sister' adds a nice absurdist escalation. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Jack: 'I'm sure her battery died right after I finished that speech, just like I wanted it to.' Then someone says 'Smooth move, Ferguson!' in the background.
jokes.setup: Jack delivers an impassioned speech to Avery about controlling their fate; the call cuts out
jokes.punchline: Jack's dignified rationalization that the timing was perfect — she heard everything important and then disconnected — is immediately punctured by a background 'Smooth move, Ferguson!'
jokes.explanation: Two jokes in one. Jack's deadpan self-delusion ('just like I wanted it to') is good character comedy, then the background 'Smooth move, Ferguson' punctures it as a perfect running-gag callback. The tonal whiplash is excellent — from high drama to absurdist background joke.

jokes.text: Tracy's breakdown: 'I came back, and you were fine without me. You laughed without me! And that was our special thing.'
jokes.setup: Tracy finally confronts the real reason the inside joke upsets him
jokes.punchline: He's hurt not by the joke itself but by the revelation that his entourage can have joy without him — 'You laughed without me! And that was our special thing.'
jokes.explanation: The emotional core of the Tracy plot lands as comedy. 'Laughing was our special thing' reveals that Tracy doesn't see comedy as universal — he sees it as something that belongs TO him. The entourage's joy without him is a betrayal. This is Tracy Jordan's most coherent character moment and it's genuinely funny because the logic is insane but emotionally recognizable.

jokes.text: Kenneth defends the inside joke: 'Smooth move Ferguson was just trying to fill a void because Mr. Slattery's political cartoons weren't cutting it.' Kenneth: 'I can't draw hands.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth is explaining how the entourage coped with Tracy's absence
jokes.punchline: Someone named Mr. Slattery was doing political cartoons as comedy, which also weren't funny — and his defense is that he can't draw hands (a common artistic struggle delivered as total non-excuse)
jokes.explanation: The 'I can't draw hands' detail is genuinely funny as a defense — it's both a real artistic challenge and a completely inadequate explanation for why political cartoons were failing as entertainment. The image of the entourage sitting through bad political cartoons while missing Tracy is endearingly absurd.

jokes.text: 'Never go away again.' Tracy: 'Don't ever tell me what to do! Quad hug, me in the middle!'
jokes.setup: The entourage tells Tracy they need him, he can never leave
jokes.punchline: Tracy's response to being told what to do is to immediately do exactly that — ordering a quad hug while pretending to resist the instruction
jokes.explanation: Perfect Tracy logic: 'Don't tell me what to do' → immediately does the warm thing they suggested while asserting authority. 'Quad hug, me in the middle' is simultaneously touching and absurd (because it's four people, requiring specification that he's in the middle). Great character integration.

jokes.text: Liz misquotes Invictus: 'No matter how much the gate is strait / or who punishes the scrolls, / I am the captain of my holes. Or whatever.'
jokes.setup: Liz triumphantly reports getting the bag, quoting Invictus as Jack taught her
jokes.punchline: Her version of the poem is completely garbled — 'punishes the scrolls,' 'captain of my holes' — delivered with full confidence before trailing off with 'or whatever'
jokes.explanation: The Invictus callback reaches its perfect conclusion. Liz's garbled version ('captain of my holes') and the dismissive 'or whatever' at the end perfectly encapsulates her relationship with Jack's highbrow inspiration — she absorbed none of it. 'Captain of my holes' is accidentally excellent. High character integration and quotability.

jokes.text: Jack: 'Condi tried, but Avery plus freedom equals... frowny face.'
jokes.setup: Jack explains that Condoleezza Rice's efforts failed
jokes.punchline: He delivers the bad news using the same emoji-equation format from his own terrible text breakup — 'frowny face'
jokes.explanation: The episode's best callback and one of its overall top jokes. The 'frowny face' equation format is reprised perfectly — and now it's not just a funny detail about a bad breakup, it's become Jack's actual emotional vocabulary. He can only express devastating news in the same reductive format. The callback rewards attention and deepens the original joke. 'Avery plus freedom equals frowny face' is brilliantly calibrated in its flatness — it conveys enormous tragedy in the most emotionally stunted possible package.

jokes.text: Final twist: Avery is now married to Kim Jong-un. 'Avery is now married to Kim Jong-il's son, Kim Jong-un.'
jokes.setup: Jack reports the hostage situation is unresolved — North Korea won't release Avery
jokes.punchline: The solution North Korea found was to marry Avery to Kim Jong-un — a plot twist of escalating absurdity that raises the stakes to maximum
jokes.explanation: The season finale twist lands well as comedy because it escalates the already absurd situation to its logical extreme. The casual delivery of this geopolitical soap opera is 30 Rock's brand. Setting up season 6 while getting a laugh is economically efficient storytelling.

jokes.text: Liz's reaction to the Avery news: 'No!' / Bag appears in the tree behind her: 'Mortality!'
jokes.setup: Liz just celebrated getting the bag; now she gets devastating news
jokes.punchline: A new bag appears in the tree and delivers a one-word callback: 'Mortality!'
jokes.explanation: The perfect capper to the bag storyline. After the bag's elaborate mortality monologue, a new bag appears and delivers the entire thesis in one word. The economy is perfect (10/10 — one word does all the work). The callback to the 'mortality' theme, combined with the visual callback of the new bag, is elegant structure. The bag wins.

jokes.text: Final 'Smooth move, Ferguson' callback — said in response to Jack's devastating news
jokes.setup: Jack receives the devastating news about Avery marrying Kim Jong-un
jokes.punchline: 'Smooth move, Ferguson' is said one final time — now functioning as a genuine expression of sympathy/irony rather than just an inside joke
jokes.explanation: The running gag's final use is the most resonant. 'Smooth move, Ferguson' — originally meaningless — now lands as a perfect ironic comment on Jack's fate. The show has imbued a nonsense phrase with emotional weight through repetition. This is how great running gags work: they become a language. The final use is earned.

jokes.text: End scene: 'Put that coffee down. Coffee's for closers only...' — characters perform scenes from Glengarry Glen Ross, Ghostbusters, Star Wars
jokes.setup: End-of-episode scene at what appears to be a sales office or meeting
jokes.punchline: Characters mashup famous movie monologues — Glengarry Glen Ross, Star Wars ('Luke, I am your father'), Ghostbusters — culminating in 'Let's go, black partner!' referencing the Tracy/Kim Jong-il film
jokes.explanation: A fun but somewhat scattershot closing sequence. The movie mashup lands the 'Let's go, black partner!' callback well, but the sequence feels more like an excuse to do impressions than a tightly constructed joke. 'Ghostbusters' as a non sequitur is intentionally absurd but slightly lazy. Above average for the episode's weakest section.

tmdb_overview: Liz tries to turn her personal life from drab to fab by revamping her dream apartment. Meanwhile, Avery is held hostage, and Tracy discovers that Kenneth, Dot Com and Grizz have forged a solid bond while he was away.
insight: Season finale delivers 64 jokes at 2.86/min—a dense meta-comedy peak.
